cacao-must-ferment-the-buried-step-that-.context_blurb:
Chocolate begins in the rainforest, on the cacao tree of West Africa and the Americas, and between the tree and the bar lies a step most chocolate lovers have never heard of. Freshly picked cacao tastes nothing like chocolate. Before it can, the farmer must let it rot a little, in a warm, bubbling heap.

Crack open a ripe, football-shaped pod and you find sweet, fruity white pulp wrapped around dozens of almond-sized seeds, and those small seeds inside, not the pulp, are what become chocolate; we call them cocoa beans. Bite a fresh seed and you are in for a shock, because it is bitter and mouth-puckering, with only a faint hint of cocoa.

The pods grow in a strange place, sprouting straight from the trunk and the thick old branches instead of from new twigs, a rare habit botanists call cauliflory. Carl Linnaeus, the Swedish naturalist who gave living things their two-word Latin names, called the tree Theobroma cacao, from two Greek words meaning 'food of the gods'.

After harvest the beans are scooped out with their pulp, heaped under banana leaves and left for about five days, and no starter is needed, because wild yeasts and bacteria already living on the pulp feast on its sugar and drive the fermentation. Inside, a raw bean is deep purple, and as it ferments those purple pigments break down, so the bean slowly turns brown.

Fermenting the beans in their heaps is where chocolate flavour is born, because it builds the sugars and amino acids that roasting will later turn into chocolate taste; skip it, and no amount of roasting will make a bean taste of chocolate. The order never changes: first the beans ferment, next they are spread out to dry in the sun, both on the farm, and only much later are they roasted.

The feasting microbes warm the heap until its core passes 50°C, hotter than a hot bath, and the heat kills each seed's embryo, so a seed that could once have sprouted into a tree never can again. That is the moment a plantable seed becomes a cocoa bean.

cacao-to-chocolate-the-bitter-money-drin.context_blurb:
Long before chocolate was a sweet bar, it was a drink, and a serious one. The Aztecs of central Mexico, and the Maya before them, drank it cold, thick, foamy and bitter, and it belonged above all to nobles, priests and warriors. Cacao beans were so valuable that they were also money, a currency you could brew and drink.

Instead of sugar, Aztec cooks spiked the drink with dried, ground chilli peppers, along with honey, vanilla or flowers, and its name in Nahuatl, the Aztec language, means roughly 'bitter water'. The Aztecs never minted coins, so shoppers paid with cacao beans: a price list from 1545 puts an avocado at three beans and a turkey hen at about a hundred.

Money invites fakes. Bernardino de Sahagún, a Spanish friar, wrote down how Aztec forgers hollowed out real cacao beans and packed the empty shells with mud or sand so they still looked real. The best part of the drink was the thick foam on top, which a server raised fresh before the drinker's eyes by pouring the chocolate back and forth between two vessels from a height. The wooden whisk people picture came later, with the Spanish.

When Carl Linnaeus gave the cacao tree its scientific name in 1753, he honoured the reverence of the Maya and the Aztecs by calling it Theobroma, Greek for 'food of the gods'.

Chocolate's savoury side survives in Puebla's mole, a deep, dark sauce of dried chillies, nuts, spices and a little bitter chocolate, ladled over turkey or chicken. Chocolate in mole is a fusion from after the Spanish conquest, since the Aztecs kept cacao for drinking.

Cacao did not even start in Mexico: in 2018 scientists who tested pottery from Ecuador, some 5,300 years old, found cacao residue and DNA, showing that the tree was first domesticated in the upper Amazon, in South America, about 1,500 years before it reached the lands of the Maya and Aztecs.

cacio-e-pepe-a-three-thing-emulsion.context_blurb:
Cacio e pepe, 'cheese and pepper', is one of Rome's oldest and simplest pasta dishes: pasta, black pepper and a hard, salty cheese, and nothing else. Out of those three things a good cook makes a glossy, creamy sauce, and Roman cooks defend the recipe's simplicity fiercely.

The cheese is pecorino romano, hard, salty and aged, and its name comes from pecora, the word for sheep, because it is made from sheep's milk rather than the cow's milk of most pasta cheeses. The sauce's creaminess comes from no cream or butter at all, but from grated cheese beaten together with the starchy water the pasta cooked in, so that fat and water hold together in a smooth, glossy coat.

Here the pepper is a main ingredient, not a garnish, so the cook toasts it for two or three minutes in a hot, dry pan before any liquid goes in, which releases the aromatic oils trapped in the peppercorns and fills the kitchen with a sharp, piney smell.

The classic disaster, cheese seizing into stringy, rubbery lumps, comes from heat: when the pasta water is close to boiling, the cheese's proteins clump together above about 65°C and squeeze out their fat, so the fix is to let the water cool a little before it meets the cheese. In 2025 a team of Italian physicists won an Ig Nobel Prize for mapping exactly this failure.

calcium-dairy-greens-and-why-spinach-lie.context_blurb:
Calcium is the most plentiful mineral in your body; a grown adult carries a couple of pounds of it. The classic sources are dairy foods and leafy greens. But the amount of calcium in a food is only half the story. What matters is how much of it your body can actually take in, and there one famous green vegetable cheats.

More than 99 percent of that calcium is locked into your bones and teeth, as a hard mineral that makes the skeleton rigid, and only a tiny fraction circulates anywhere else. In the United States the main supply comes from milk, cheese and yogurt, the dairy foods, which provide about 72 percent of the calcium people eat.

Someone who avoids dairy can still find plenty of calcium in plants, and the standouts are leafy greens and their cabbage-family cousins, such as kale, collards, bok choy and broccoli.

Spinach looks like a calcium star on paper, but it carries oxalic acid, a plant acid that binds its calcium into crystals of calcium oxalate the gut can barely absorb, so you take up only about 5 percent of it, against roughly 27 percent from milk. Canned sardines are a hidden source, because canning softens their tiny bones until you eat them without noticing, and those bones are almost pure calcium, so a single tin holds about as much calcium as a glass of milk.

Even then, the gut cannot pull much calcium into the blood without vitamin D, which escorts it across, and since the skin makes vitamin D when sunlight strikes it, it is nicknamed the sunshine vitamin. And milk, the old gold standard, has been beaten: in a 1993 study, people absorbed about 52 percent of the calcium in bok choy and about 48 percent from broccoli, against about 46 percent from milk.

canning-and-botulism-the-food-that-can-h.context_blurb:
Canning keeps food safe for years, but a badly canned jar can hide one of the deadliest poisons known. The danger is a germ called Clostridium botulinum, which cannot stand acid, oxygen or high heat but thrives in a sealed, airless jar that was not heated enough. Commercial canneries follow strict rules that keep the risk tiny; home canners have to learn them.

Canning began with a prize. Around 1800 France's government offered 12,000 francs for a way to keep army food from rotting, and in 1810 a Paris confectioner, Nicolas Appert, collected it after some fourteen years of trials. His method was to seal food inside glass jars and then boil the sealed jars, the direct ancestor of every canned food on a store shelf.

Appert never knew why it worked; decades later Louis Pasteur showed that the boiling kills the tiny living germs that make food go bad, while the seal keeps new ones out. The worst of those germs gave its illness a gruesome name, for 'botulism' comes from botulus, the Latin word for sausage: in the 1700s and 1800s, Germans kept dying after eating spoiled blood sausages, and doctors named the 'sausage poisoning' long before anyone found the germ behind it.

The botulism toxin is so powerful that a speck too small to see can kill an adult, because it blocks the signals from nerves to muscles, yet in tiny, purified doses that same muscle-freezing effect is sold as Botox injections. Honey can carry sleeping botulism spores, which an older child's or adult's gut crowds out harmlessly, but a baby less than a year old lacks that protection, so doctors say never to give honey to infants under twelve months.

The spores are armoured well enough to survive a pot of water boiling at 212°F. Acidic foods such as pickles and jam can still be canned in boiling water, because their acid stops the spores from growing. Low-acid foods like green beans, corn and meat lack that shield, so they must go into a pressure canner, which traps steam until the jars reach about 240°F, hot enough to kill the spores. Low-acid vegetables canned without one cause more botulism outbreaks in the United States than anything else.

Poisoned food gives no warning to the eyes, nose or tongue, but the growing germ gives off gas, and the gas pushes the lid outward, so a swollen, bulging lid is the warning sign to throw the jar away. When in doubt, throw it out.

cantonese-cooking-dim-sum-and-the-steame.context_blurb:
In Hong Kong and across Cantonese southern China, families gather for a long, noisy late-morning meal of little dumplings, buns and small dishes, wheeled between the tables on carts or stacked in bamboo baskets. The food is dim sum, the outing has a name of its own, and the Cantonese cooking behind it prizes freshness above all.

Cantonese families call the outing yum cha, which means 'drink tea', because the tea matters as much as the food; the old shorthand for the meal was 'one cup, two pieces'.

The little dishes themselves are dim sum, a name that means 'touch the heart', for bites meant to delight rather than to make a full meal. When a friend refills your teacup, you thank him without a word by tapping two fingers twice on the table, because the room is loud and your mouth is probably full. Legend says the gesture began when the emperor Qianlong, travelling in disguise, poured tea for his servants, who could not bow without giving him away and so bowed with their fingers instead.

The pink shrimp dumpling har gow is called the crystal dumpling because its wrapper is made from wheat starch rather than ordinary flour, so it steams glassy and clear, showing the curled shrimp inside. Har gow is one of the Four Heavenly Kings of dim sum, along with siu mai, little open dumplings of pork and prawn; char siu bao, soft buns of barbecued pork; and the sweet egg tart.

Cantonese cooks trust fresh ingredients so much that a whole fish is simply steamed until it flakes and then finished with a little soy sauce, shreds of ginger and scallion, and a splash of hot oil, never drowned in a heavy sauce.

Steaming itself has a legend: around 200 BCE, the story goes, the Han general Han Xin fed his army inside a cramped barracks by having his cooks build stacked cookers of bamboo and wood, heated by steam, the ancestor of the bamboo steamer. Steaming is truly ancient, for clay steamers about 7,000 years old have been dug up at the Banpo site.

capsaicin-and-trpv1-the-burn-that-isnt-h.context_blurb:
Chilli peppers came from the Americas, where Mexican and Andean farmers bred them for thousands of years before Columbus's voyages spread them round the world. A raw chilli on the counter is no warmer than an apple, yet one bite sets the mouth ablaze. The burn is a trick, played on a nerve sensor that exists for a very different job.

Behind the burn of every hot chilli, from a mild jalapeño to a ghost pepper, is one molecule, capsaicin, which a German chemist first drew out of peppers in 1816. Capsaicin does no real damage; it tricks the nerves in your mouth into reporting heat, so you feel scalded while a thermometer on your tongue would read normal.

Most cooks blame the seeds, but the seeds make no capsaicin at all: the heat is packed into the pale ribs and pith inside the pod where the seeds attach, so cutting out the ribs is what really tames a chilli. The sensor capsaicin hijacks is called TRPV1, and its real job is to warn you when something is dangerously hot, firing above about 43°C (109°F), so chilli sets off the very same burning alarm as scalding soup.

Gulping cold water barely helps, because capsaicin is oily and will not mix with water, so the water just smears it around. Milk works far better, thanks to casein, a milk protein that wraps around the oily capsaicin and lifts it off the tongue's sensors; in one test skim milk worked as well as whole milk, a sign that the protein, not the fat, does the job. And because TRPV1 is a genuine heat sensor, real warmth and capsaicin set off the very same receptor, which is why a hot sauce tastes fiercer stirred into steaming soup than straight from the fridge.

Birds feel nothing from capsaicin, because their version of the sensor ignores it, and that is the plant's plan: birds gulp the seeds down whole and drop them far away, still able to grow, while chewing mammals, which crush seeds, are warned off by the burn. In 1912 the pharmacist Wilbur Scoville built his famous heat scale by dissolving a pepper's extract in alcohol and then diluting it with sugar water until tasters could no longer feel any burn; the more dilution it took, the higher the score.

Real pain with no real injury makes the brain answer with endorphins, its own natural painkillers, the same chemicals behind a runner's high, which is why some people chase hotter and hotter sauces; the psychologist Paul Rozin called the habit benign masochism. Capsaicin can even relieve pain, because repeated exposure wears the TRPV1 sensors out until they stop firing, a process called desensitisation, which is why doctors put capsaicin into creams for aching joints and nerve pain.

car-me-and-edible-architecture.context_blurb:
Marie-Antoine Carême was the most celebrated cook on the continent in the early 1800s, cooking for Napoleon, for the future King George IV of Britain and for the richest tables of his age. He began as a pastry cook who longed to be an architect, and he treated pastry as a kind of building. The towers he raised above banquet tables made him a legend.

His centrepieces, the pièces montées, rose several feet above the candles and wax fruit of a banquet table, and unlike every other ornament there they were made of food, edible to the last crumb. Flowers, wax and silver could decorate a table, but a pièce montée was the one sculpture there you were allowed to build out of dinner. The best-known survivor of that tradition is the croquembouche, a cone-shaped tower of cream puffs still brought out for French weddings, baptisms and Christmas. It is never left plain, for it comes dressed like a little monument, studded with chocolate, edible flowers and sugared almonds.

His favourite models were famous buildings, so a diner might recognise a pagoda from China, a pyramid from Egypt or a temple from Greece, rebuilt several feet high in sugar. For stone, mortar and glass he used a pastry cook's materials instead: confectioner's paste, spun sugar, marzipan and nougat. Carême even changed what chefs wear, making the tall, starched white toque standard, reportedly because the old floppy caps made cooks look ill.

To get the buildings right, he spent the two free afternoons a week his employer gave him in the print rooms of the national library in Paris, copying engravings of architecture. His savoury masterpiece was the vol-au-vent, a light-as-air hollow case of puff pastry filled with a creamy ragout. Legend says an amazed assistant, watching one rise in the oven, cried that it was flying on the wind, vol-au-vent, and the name stuck, though the phrase appears in a cookbook from 1739, before Carême was born.

He listed five fine arts, with architecture among them, and then declared that architecture's principal branch was confectionery, the making of sweets and pastry. The croquembouche takes its name from the old French phrase croque en bouche, 'crunch in the mouth', for the crackle of its hard caramel. Carême featured it in his book of 1815, Le Pâtissier royal parisien, and he is the chef most linked to it.

Every croquembouche is made of one repeated brick, little choux puffs filled with cream and stuck together with threads of spun caramel, which makes it edible architecture in its purest form.

caramelized-onions-and-french-onion-soup.context_blurb:
French onion soup is a bowl of beef broth, onions, bread and melted cheese, and its deep brown colour and sweetness do not come from the broth at all. They come from the onions, and from one patient technique. That technique, caramelising, is a piece of kitchen chemistry that also browns crème brûlée and tarte Tatin.

The cook takes plain, sharp onions and cooks them slowly in butter over low, gentle heat until they turn deep golden-brown and soft as jam, and only then adds the beef stock, so the soup takes its colour and sweetness straight from them. Recipes that promise caramelised onions in five or ten minutes are lying, as the food writer Tom Scocca complained, because real caramelising takes three-quarters of an hour to an hour on medium-low heat, and anything faster gives you merely softened onions.

A Paris bistro tops the soup with a slice of stale baguette, buries it under grated Gruyère and slides the crock under the grill until the cheese bubbles into a molten brown lid. This gratinée finish was born in the mid-1800s around Les Halles, the great Paris food market, where the soup fed porters at dawn.

The browning of the onions is caramelization, sugar breaking down under heat into brown, nutty-tasting compounds, and it is the same reaction that gives crème brûlée its crackly amber top and tarte Tatin its golden apples. A seared steak browns too, though it is not sweet, through a different reaction, the Maillard reaction, which needs the amino acids of protein as well as sugar; it also browns bread crust and roasting coffee.

The famous story of tarte Tatin, in which the overworked Stéphanie Tatin burned her apples in the 1880s and rescued them by baking the tart upside down, is mostly legend, attached to the sisters years later. They never named the dish or wrote down a recipe, and the name was given after their deaths by the food writer Curnonsky and the Paris restaurant Maxim's.

carbohydrates-smart-vs-empty-fiber-and-b.context_blurb:
Not all carbohydrates behave the same once you eat them. A glass of juice and a whole apple, or white bread and whole-grain bread, carry similar carbs but treat your body very differently. The difference lies in the parts of the plant that refining throws away, above all the stringy part you cannot digest: fibre.

A whole apple and a glass of its juice carry about the same sugar, but the apple also holds about 4 grams of fibre, which slows the sugar's journey into the blood, while the juice has almost none and sends blood sugar spiking. Pressing takes three or four apples to fill one cup, concentrating the sugar and throwing the fibre away.

Refining grain strips more than fibre. Milling wheat into white flour discards the germ, the tiny living core of the seed, and with it goes about 90 percent of the grain's vitamin E, along with more than half of its B vitamins. Whole-grain bread, brown rice and oats keep them.

Fibre you cannot digest still feeds you, through the trillions of microbes in your large intestine. They ferment it into butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid, and butyrate is the favourite fuel of the cells that line your colon. In one experiment, mice on a high-fibre diet that also carried butyrate-making bacteria grew 75 percent fewer colon tumours; without those bacteria, the fibre gave no protection.

carbonara-egg-not-cream.context_blurb:
Spaghetti carbonara is one of Rome's great pasta dishes, and one of the most often faked. It looks so rich that diners assume it is full of cream. In fact the sauce is egg, cheese, black pepper and crisp cured pork, turned silky by nothing but the heat of the pasta. Even its history is younger than it looks.

A real carbonara never contains cream: its creaminess comes from beaten egg and grated cheese, warmed by the hot pasta and loosened with a splash of its starchy cooking water. The cheese is Pecorino Romano, sharp and salty, made from sheep's milk, since pecora means sheep in Italian, rather than the Parmesan tourists expect. The last essential is coarsely cracked black pepper, which lends each mouthful its warm bite.

Bacon and pancetta come from the pig's belly, but a Roman carbonara uses guanciale, cured pork cheek, fattier and more intensely porky, whose rendered fat melts into the sauce.

The name comes from carbone, coal, and means 'in the manner of the charcoal burners', though the romantic tale that charcoal burners invented it in the woods is unproven folklore. Carbonara has three Roman cousins, all built from the same pantry: cacio e pepe is cheese and pepper, gricia adds guanciale, amatriciana is gricia with tomato, and carbonara is gricia with egg, so gricia, carbonara without its egg, is nicknamed 'white amatriciana'.

The classic mistake is cooking the sauce over a flame, which scrambles the egg into gritty lumps; the cook should take the pan off the heat and let the warmth of the pasta, with a little starchy water, thicken the egg into a smooth, glossy sauce. As for its age, no Italian cookbook before the Second World War mentions carbonara, and it first turns up in Rome after the city's liberation in 1944; the leading theory says Roman cooks improvised it from the eggs and bacon in American army rations, adding local pasta, pecorino and pepper.

carbs-are-fuel-simple-complex-and-the-gl.context_blurb:
Carbohydrates, the sugars and starches in bread, rice, potatoes and fruit, are the body's quickest fuel. They start as stored sunlight, travel through your blood as one small sugar, and get packed away for later in a dense molecule that athletes know all about. When that store runs out mid-race, the body hits a wall.

Every carb began in a plant, which used the energy of sunlight to stitch carbon dioxide and water into sugar and starch, so the energy in bread or an apple is sunlight the plant captured. Almost all life, from bacteria to your own brain cells, burns one small sugar as its main fuel: glucose.

Dietitians sort carbs by speed: simple carbs, the small sugar molecules in candy, honey and fruit, hit the blood fast, while complex carbs, the starch in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes, must be broken down first and release their energy slowly. The sweetest natural sugar is fructose, the fruit sugar of mangoes, honey and berries, roughly one and a half times as sweet as table sugar, and the liver handles most of it.

The greediest customer is the brain, which makes up about 2 percent of body weight yet uses about 20 percent of the body's energy, nearly all of it from glucose, some 120 grams a day. Nutritionists rank foods on a glycemic index by how sharply they spike blood sugar and let it crash, and sugary candy such as jelly beans scores high, while lentils, nuts and eggs score low and give steady energy. Starch, the main carb in pasta, is nothing but glucose molecules linked into a long chain, which is why runners eat a big pasta dinner the night before a race to stock up.

Glucose you do not need right away is packed into glycogen, a tightly branched molecule that is the animal answer to the starch of plants, kept in the liver and muscles and built to release glucose fast. Your blood holds surprisingly little sugar at any moment, only about 4 grams in the whole bloodstream, about a teaspoon, and the liver tops it up from its glycogen between meals, which carries you through a night's sleep.

Some twenty miles into a marathon, when the glycogen in a runner's muscles and liver runs dry, crushing exhaustion strikes all at once, with legs like lead and a sinking spirit, and runners call that moment hitting the wall. Yet carbs are the body's default fuel, not its only one: when glucose runs low, the liver breaks body fat into ketones, a backup fuel that even the glucose-hungry brain learns to burn, supplying up to 30 or 40 percent of its energy after a three-day fast.

cardamom-the-fragrant-pods.context_blurb:
Cardamom comes as small, papery green pods no longer than a thumbnail, and it is one of the most fragrant spices in the world. It flavours coffee across the Middle East, anchors India's garam masala and sweetens Swedish buns. Its home is the rainforest of southern India, where it has been traded for more than a thousand years.

The pod is only a wrapper: split it open and inside lies the real spice, a little cluster of fifteen to twenty sticky black seeds packed in three neat rows. A crushed seed smells warm and a little peppery, a clue to its family, for cardamom belongs to the ginger family and is a close cousin of ginger itself.

Indians love cardamom so much that they eat most of their own harvest, so the world's biggest exporter today is Guatemala, where, the story goes, a German coffee planter brought seeds from India in 1914; by about 1980 Guatemala had overtaken India, and Guatemalans call the crop green gold.

Only saffron and vanilla cost more by weight, and the reason is labour: the pods on one bush ripen at different times, so pickers must comb the same plants by hand three or four times a season, plucking each pod at its peak, a job no machine can do.

The most surprising cardamom lovers live in Scandinavia, where Swedes eat about sixty times as much of it as Americans, in cardamom buns and Christmas baking. A popular legend says Vikings found the spice in Constantinople a thousand years ago and carried it home, though some historians think it arrived later, by way of Moorish Spain.

cassava-the-poison-staple-you-have-to-de.context_blurb:
Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, is a starchy tropical root that more than 500 million people depend on, especially in Africa. It is hardy, cheap and filling. It is also poisonous when raw, and the traditional ways of grating, soaking and cooking it are what make it safe.

The chewy pearls in bubble tea come from cassava, for they are tapioca, a nearly pure starch washed out of the root, free of its fibre and its poison. Raw bitter cassava hides compounds that release cyanide, one of the most notorious poisons in the world, when the root is chewed or crushed.

Cassava is not African at all; it is a crop of South America, native to Brazil and its neighbours, and Portuguese traders carried it to Africa from the late 1500s.

When drought or famine pushes families to rush the soaking, leftover cyanide can cause konzo, which suddenly and permanently paralyses the legs, mostly in children and young women; the name comes from the Yaka people of Congo and means 'tied legs'. Many farmers still plant the bitter kind on purpose, though it can carry fifty times the poison of sweet cassava, because its toxin drives away pests, grazing animals and thieves, and careful processing makes it safe to eat.

Oddly, an uncut raw root does little harm, because in its intact cells the poison, linamarin, is kept apart from the enzyme that breaks it down, but grating or chewing ruptures the cells, the enzyme meets the poison, and cyanide is set free. That is why the traditional method grates the root hard before soaking and roasting it.

casu-marzu-the-cheese-that-is-alive.context_blurb:
Casu marzu, 'rotten cheese' in the Sardinian language, is one of the most startling foods in Europe. Shepherds on the Italian island of Sardinia make it from an ordinary wheel of sheep's-milk pecorino, and Sardinians eat it while it is still moving. Its fans prize its fierce, strong flavour; most outsiders prize the story.

The cheese is alive with fly maggots, the larvae of the cheese fly, placed in the wheel on purpose, and a single serving can hold thousands of them. Disturbed, they can flick themselves about six inches into the air, so diners shield their faces with a hand.

The maggots do the cheesemaking: as they tunnel through a hard wheel of pecorino, their digestion breaks down the cheese's fat, and over a few weeks the firm cheese collapses into a creamy, runny paste with an intensely strong flavour. They are not contamination; they are the ripening.

No shop sells casu marzu, not even in Sardinia, because the law forbids its sale: Italy outlawed it in 1962, and the European Union banned selling it in 2002, judging the live larvae a health risk. It survives anyway, passed from hand to hand as an underground tradition, and Sardinia has moved to protect it as a traditional food.

century-egg-the-egg-cured-without-heat.context_blurb:
A Chinese century egg seems ancient: its white has turned into a dark, glassy jelly and its yolk into a creamy grey-green, as if it had lain underground for a hundred years. In fact it is an ordinary raw egg, usually a duck's, transformed by chemistry. No fire, stove or boiling water ever touches it.

Despite the name, and its cousins 'thousand-year egg' and 'millennium egg', the real cure takes only several weeks to a few months; the name is pure poetry. Makers pack the raw egg in a paste of clay, wood ash, salt and quicklime, often rolled in rice hulls, and let the coating do all the work. The cure gives off ammonia and hydrogen sulphide, the rotten-egg gas, so a good century egg is pungent enough that Thai and Lao cooks bluntly call it the horse urine egg.

The paste works because it is strongly alkaline, a strong base that pushes the egg's pH up to between 9 and 12, and like the heat of a frying pan, that alkalinity unfolds the egg's proteins and locks them into a new shape, so the white sets firm without ever being warmed.

The same alkaline coating preserves the egg, because it makes the inside far too hostile for spoilage microbes to grow, so a century egg keeps for months on a shelf without a fridge. It is not rotten or fermented but preserved, in the same old family as salted fish and pickled vegetables.

ceviche-acid-that-cooks-fish-without-hea.context_blurb:
Ceviche is Peru's national dish: chunks of raw fish that arrive at the table white, firm and opaque, looking fully cooked. No flame, stove or pot of hot water has touched them. The cooking was done by acid, and that trick, simple as it sounds, has a long history and one important limit.

The fish is 'cooked' by a bath of fresh lime juice, whose acid firms the raw flesh and turns it opaque, so it looks just as if it had been on the stove.

Acid does to the fish's proteins what heat does, breaking the bonds that hold each protein folded, so the long chains unravel and then set in a new shape, and the flesh ends up firm and opaque by either route. It works on fish in minutes, while a raw steak in the same bath would stay tough, because fish muscle is made of short, delicate fibres with very little of the tough connective tissue that stiffens beef and pork.

But lime is not fire: the acid never kills the bacteria or parasites in the fish, so ceviche must be made from very fresh fish and eaten at once, never saved for tomorrow. Nothing is wasted, though, for the cloudy, tangy marinade left in the bowl, lime and fish juices with onion, garlic and chilli, is drunk from a glass as leche de tigre, which means 'tiger's milk', and is said to cure a hangover.

In Lima the classic choice is corvina, a firm white sea bass, dressed with sliced red onion, aji chilli and coriander, and eaten beside sweet potato and corn on the cob.

Limes themselves came to Peru only with the Spanish after Columbus, yet coastal people were souring raw fish some 2,000 years ago: the Moche used the fermented juice of tumbo, a passion fruit native to the region, and the Spanish simply swapped in lime and bitter orange. The story is retold as culinary legend.

cheese-and-the-first-dairying.context_blurb:
Fresh milk sours within a day. Thousands of years ago, early farmers learned to turn it into something firmer, saltier and far longer-lasting: cheese. Archaeologists and chemists have since tracked that discovery through pierced pots, an Egyptian tomb and the slow spread of a gene.

Cheese gave milk the one thing it lacked, a long life, because milk drained and salted into a firm curd became a food people could keep and carry for weeks or months.

The oldest cheese-making tools ever found came out of the ground in Kuyavia, Poland: clay vessels roughly seventy-five centuries old, punched full of holes like a colander. Those holes let the watery whey drain away while the solid curds stayed behind in the pot. A classic legend explains how cheese began. A desert traveller carried his milk in a canteen made from a young animal's dried stomach, and by the time he stopped to drink, he found his milk turned to curds and whey. The legend points at real chemistry, for the stomach lining of a young, milk-fed calf or kid holds rennet, the enzyme cheesemakers still use to curdle milk.

One of the oldest lumps of real cheese ever found, about 3,200 years old, lay in a broken jar in the tomb of Ptahmes, mayor of Memphis and a high official under the pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II, buried with him as a prized gift for the afterlife. Most early farmers, like many people today, could not digest lactose, the sugar in fresh milk, yet they ate cheese and yogurt happily, because draining away the whey removes much of the lactose and fermentation breaks down the rest. The gene that lets adults digest fresh milk spread across Europe only much later.

Proving that the Polish pots once held dairy took chemistry: milk itself rots away, but traces of the milk's fat had soaked into the porous clay and survived some 7,000 years, and in 2012 chemists identified them as dairy fat. The Egyptian cheese told a darker story, for proteins left in it showed it once carried the bacteria of brucellosis, a disease still passed on today through unpasteurized dairy. Today pasteurization, heating the milk gently, kills those bacteria, which is why store-bought milk is safe to drink.

cheese-milk-that-keeps-for-years.context_blurb:
Fresh milk is one of the most perishable foods in any kitchen, yet cheese made from that same milk can last for years in a cool cellar. The difference comes from what cheesemakers do to the milk's water, its proteins and the living things that grow in it. People have been doing it for thousands of years.

A hard wheel of Parmesan keeps for years while a soft Brie spoils in weeks, because the hard cheese has had far more of its water pressed out, and the drier a cheese is, the longer it lasts.

Legend says cheese was discovered by a desert trader who carried his milk in a pouch made from a young animal's stomach and found it set into lumps by nightfall. It is only a legend, but the chemistry is real, because the lining of a young animal's stomach holds rennet, the enzyme that sets milk into cheese.

Stir rennet into warm milk and within minutes it splits in two, because the enzyme snips the casein proteins so they clump with the fat into solid curds, while a watery liquid, the whey, drains away. That split is the heart of every cheese. The oldest cheese ever identified, about 3,600 years old, was found with Bronze Age mummies in the desert of the Tarim Basin in western China, and in 2024 its DNA showed a kefir cheese made from cow and goat milk, laid with the dead as food for the afterlife.

Blue cheese gets its veins on purpose: the blue mould, Penicillium roqueforti, needs oxygen, so the cheesemaker pokes needles all through the young wheel to open air channels, and the mould grows along those lines.

chicago-beef-the-cold-railcar-that-centr.context_blurb:
In the 1870s, Chicago sat at the centre of America's cattle trade, with the herds of the western plains on one side and the hungry cities of the East on the other. Meatpackers there worked out how to slaughter cattle in one place and ship only the chilled meat, and the change transformed the way Americans ate. It also helped invent the modern factory.

Before refrigeration, a western steer bound for a Boston butcher usually travelled alive, crammed into a cattle car for days; the animals lost weight, got bruised, and some died, and most of each one was bone, hide and innards nobody could eat. The meatpacker Gustavus Swift had a better plan, to slaughter the herds in Chicago and ship just the beef east in a refrigerated railcar kept cold with blocks of ice, so that one cold car could replace a whole cattle car of live animals.

In 1878 Swift hired the engineer Andrew Chase, who put the ice in bins across the roof of the car so the cold air would sink evenly through the whole load, with the beef stacked low to keep the car steady. Speed came from the killing floor, where, from 1867, Philip Armour gave each worker a single cut to make again and again as carcasses came past, a 'disassembly line' that took an animal apart instead of building something up. By 1916 the stockyards were so much the symbol of the city that the poet Carl Sandburg opened his poem 'Chicago' by calling it Hog Butcher for the World.

America's big railroads, which had sunk fortunes into cattle cars and stockyard pens, refused to haul Swift's cold cars, so he struck a deal with the Grand Trunk Railway and sent his beef north through Canada and back down to the East Coast. The packing houses even inspired Henry Ford, who wrote in 1922 that his moving assembly line grew from the overhead trolley the Chicago packers used to roll carcasses past their workers. Swift proudly said his cold cars had opened an era of cheap beef, when fresh beef could reach families far from any ranch, in any season.

Swift's cars were early links in a cold chain, the unbroken run of refrigeration from killing floor to kitchen. Engineers count such a chain as broken if even one link fails, because during a few warm hours bacteria multiply on the meat, and chilling it again only stops the clock; it does not undo the growth.

chili-heat-capsaicin-and-the-scoville-sc.context_blurb:
Chillies came from the Americas and conquered the world's kitchens in barely five centuries. Their fire is measured on the Scoville scale, invented in 1912 by the American pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, which runs from zero for the mildest pepper into the millions for the fiercest. Behind every number is one molecule, and a nerve it fools.

That molecule is capsaicin, which does not burn or damage you at all; it simply fools your nerves into reporting a burn. At the bottom of the scale sits the bell pepper, which makes no capsaicin whatsoever and scores zero, while a jalapeño scores a few thousand units and a Carolina Reaper more than a million.

Capsaicin trips the nerve alarm meant for burning heat, a sensor called TRPV1 that normally fires when you touch something hotter than about 43°C (110°F), so as far as that nerve can tell, a hot chilli and a hot stove feel the same. To tame a chilli, cut out the pale inner rib, the spongy pith the seeds cling to, because that is where most of the capsaicin is made, and the seeds get most of the blame unfairly.

Not everything on the Scoville chart is food, for pepper spray, carried by police and hikers for self-defence, rates from half a million to five million units, because it is concentrated capsaicin, chilli turned into a weapon. All chillies come from the Americas, where people were already eating them by about 7,500 BC and farmers in Mexico, Peru and Bolivia later domesticated them. Hungarian paprika, the deep-red powder of goulash, is nothing but mild or sweet chillies, dried and ground, and Spain smokes the same peppers over oak to make pimentón.

Columbus's crew, meeting the fiery Caribbean pods in 1492, borrowed the name of black pepper, the costly Asian spice, even though the two plants are unrelated, and chillies have been called peppers ever since. Modern breeders chase ever more heat: Ed Currie, who bred the Carolina Reaper, spent a full decade crossing about a hundred kinds of pepper every year to create Pepper X, which Guinness named the world's hottest in 2023, at about 2.7 million units. Scoville's own test was done by tongue: he steeped a pepper in alcohol, then kept thinning the extract with sugared water until a panel of tasters could no longer feel any burn, and the count of dilutions was the pepper's rating. Machines took over the job in the 1980s.

The fire of curry, Thai cooking and Sichuan food is less than five hundred years old, because Portuguese traders carried chillies out of the Americas and into Asia in the 1500s; the first Chinese mention of chilli dates only from 1591. When a curry sets your mouth ablaze, water barely helps, since oily capsaicin will not dissolve in it, but milk works, because its protein, casein, acts like a soap that lifts the capsaicin off your nerves and rinses it away. Birds feel no burn at all, because their version of the heat sensor ignores capsaicin, and that is the plant's design: birds swallow the fruit and drop the seeds whole and far away, while seed-crushing mammals are driven off.

chilis-journey-into-asia-the-columbian-e.context_blurb:
Chillies burn in kitchens from India to Korea to Hungary, and it is hard to imagine those cuisines without them. Yet five hundred years ago no cook in Asia had ever tasted one. The chilli's journey across the oceans is one of the great stories of the Columbian Exchange, the swap of foods between the hemispheres that followed Columbus.

A chilli's fire comes from capsaicin, which warms nothing at all; it binds to pain sensors in the mouth and fools the brain into feeling burned while the tissue stays unharmed.

Chillies were domesticated in the Americas, in central Mexico and in the highlands and lowlands of South America, roughly 6,000 years ago, and they reached Asia only after Columbus opened the sea routes. The Portuguese carried them east: their spice ships, sailing Vasco da Gama's route round Africa, brought chillies from Brazil to their Indian colony of Goa and on across Asia in the 1500s, and within a century Indian and Sichuan cooks were using them.

Before chilli came, Sichuan's 'spicy' food leaned on the Sichuan peppercorn, a native berry that does not burn at all but makes the lips and tongue tingle and go numb, a sensation called má; paired with chilli's fiery là, it gives Sichuan cooking its famous málà. China's first written mention of the chilli, from 1591, treats it not as food but as a decorative houseplant, admired for its looks, and Chinese cooks did not use it for about another century. Korea's kimchi, now famous for its red fire, was pale white for most of its history, a dish of vegetables in a light salt brine; chilli reached Korea only around 1600, and red kimchi became common in the 1800s.

Most of a chilli's heat lives in the white inner rib, the pith the seeds cling to, which holds the great majority of the capsaicin, so slicing it out tames the fire; the belief that the heat is all in the seeds is a myth. In 1912 the pharmacist Wilbur Scoville found the first way to measure that heat, with no lab machines at all: he thinned a pepper's extract with sugar water, over and over, until his tasters could feel no burn, and the more dilution it took, the hotter the pepper. The burn is aimed at mammals, which grind seeds to dust, while birds, whose pain sensor ignores capsaicin, eat chillies freely and scatter the seeds unharmed in their droppings.

In the 1980s the psychologist Paul Rozin studied chilli-loving villagers in Mexico and concluded that the taste is learned, not inborn, because people train themselves to like the burn a little at a time, creeping up on more heat. He named the enjoyment of such harmless pain benign masochism, the same pull that draws people to sad films and roller coasters.

chocolate-from-bitter-aztec-drink-to-swe.context_blurb:
For most of its history chocolate was not a candy at all. Among the Aztecs and Maya of Mexico and Central America it was a bitter, spicy drink made from ground cacao beans, and the beans themselves were money. Spanish conquerors carried it to Europe in the 1500s, where cooks slowly sweetened it, and the solid bar is less than two hundred years old.

For some three thousand years chocolate was strictly a frothy drink, ground cacao beaten up with water, and a bar you could bite came along only in the 1800s. The Aztec version, xocolatl, had no sugar and tasted bitter, and it was often spiced with ground chilli peppers.

Europeans soon learned how highly the tree was prized, and in 1753 Carl Linnaeus named it Theobroma, from Greek words meaning 'food of the gods'. Cacao beans were real money, and according to a price list from 1545, a single bean bought a ripe avocado or a large tomato, while bigger purchases cost dozens or hundreds of beans.

The foam was the best part of the drink, and with no whisk at all, Aztec servers raised it by pouring the chocolate from a height, back and forth between two tall cups. Many Spaniards disliked the bitter, foamy drink for decades, until Europeans remade it for their own tastes, and the addition that mattered most was sugar.

Where there is money there are forgers, and the Florentine Codex, a record of Aztec life compiled by the friar Bernardino de Sahagún, describes cheats who emptied real cacao shells and repacked them with ash, dough or wax. The emperor Montezuma II drank chocolate in staggering style: the Spanish soldier Bernal Díaz wrote that servants brought him more than fifty pitchers at a sitting, in golden cups that he used only a single time. The first Europeans to meet cacao, Columbus's crew in 1502, had no idea it was money, but when some beans spilled from a captured Maya trading canoe, a Spanish account says the Maya snatched them up as if an eye had fallen.

Chocolate stayed a drink because ground cacao will not set into a smooth solid by itself, and the breakthrough was Coenraad van Houten's press of 1828, which squeezed the fatty cocoa butter out of the beans and left solids that could be ground into cocoa powder. Later makers melted cocoa butter back into cocoa and sugar to make a paste that could be moulded into bars. Those first bars were gritty. Rodolphe Lindt, a Swiss chocolatier, fixed that in 1879 without adding anything: he stirred the chocolate for hours on end, a process called conching, and the long stirring gave it the smooth melt that fine bars are known for.

chocolate-is-a-bitter-fermented-roasted-.context_blurb:
A chocolate bar is sweet, smooth and ready to melt. Nothing about the plant it comes from would predict that. Chocolate begins as the hard, bitter seed of a tropical tree, and it passes through several surprising changes, on the farm and in the factory, before it tastes like chocolate at all.

The cacao tree of the hot, wet lowlands of Central and South America grows its heavy, football-shaped pods straight from its trunk and its thickest branches, not out at the twig tips, a habit called cauliflory that puts the pods low enough to cut by hand. Each pod holds dozens of beans packed in slippery white pulp, and that pulp is a treat in itself, bright and fruity with a citrus tang, often compared to lychee or lemonade, so in the tropics it is eaten as a snack.

The raw bean, though, is sharply bitter, with none of the flavour of a chocolate bar. That flavour has to be built: the beans ferment for several days in their own pulp, then are dried, then roasted, which tames the bitterness and creates the hundreds of aroma compounds we know as chocolate.

When the Spanish arrived in the early 1500s, they found the Aztecs and Maya drinking their chocolate bitter and unsweetened, usually spiced with dried, ground chilli; sugar and milk were added only after chocolate reached Europe. White chocolate is pale because it contains only cocoa butter, the fat of the bean, with sugar and milk, and none of the brown cocoa solids, so it can never turn brown.

Ground roasted beans make a thick, greasy paste, and in 1828 the Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten patented a powerful press that squeezes the fat, the cocoa butter, out of it, leaving a dry cake that is ground into cocoa powder. Cocoa butter and cocoa powder are the two halves of one bean, and chocolate makers recombine them, with sugar and sometimes milk, in different proportions.

cholesterol-and-the-eggs-comeback.context_blurb:
For decades doctors warned against eggs, since a yolk is loaded with cholesterol, the substance blamed for clogged arteries. Over the past twenty years nutrition science has largely reversed itself on that point, and the egg has quietly returned to the breakfast table. The real story of cholesterol turned out to be more interesting than the scare.

Almost all of an egg's cholesterol sits in the golden yolk, along with its fat and fat-soluble vitamins, while the white is mostly protein and water, so the yolk was exactly the part the old advice told people to cut.

The whole egg scare rested on an intuitive idea, that eating cholesterol raises the cholesterol in your blood almost one for one. Measured, the idea fell apart, because only about a fifth of the cholesterol in your blood comes from food, and your own body makes the other four-fifths, mostly in the liver, which turns out some 800 milligrams a day against about 186 in a large egg.

The liver also senses what you eat: after a big breakfast of eggs and bacon, it throttles back its own production to make up for the extra, a feedback loop that partly cancels out the meal.

So in 2015 the American dietary guidelines dropped their long-standing numeric cap of 300 milligrams of cholesterol a day, after nearly half a century, though they did not declare cholesterol irrelevant to health. The bigger driver of LDL cholesterol in the blood turned out to be saturated fat, which hampers the liver's ability to clear LDL. Whether raising LDL this way actually drives heart disease is itself still debated, since several later analyses failed to confirm the link.

Cholesterol is no poison but a raw material the body cannot live without: it builds every cell membrane, helps make vitamin D and the bile that digests fat, and is the starting point for all the steroid hormones, from cortisol to testosterone and oestrogen.

choux-pastry-eclairs-and-cream-puffs.context_blurb:
Choux pastry is the French dough behind éclairs, cream puffs and profiteroles. It breaks almost every rule of baking: it is cooked before it is baked, it rises with no yeast and no baking powder, and it comes out of the oven as a crisp shell around nothing at all. That emptiness is the whole point.

A baked cream puff is a thin, crisp shell wrapped around a big hollow centre, a built-in cup that the pastry chef fills with custard or cream through one small hole. 'Choux' is the French word for cabbage, because a piped blob of the dough puffs into a bumpy little ball that reminded French bakers of a small round cabbage.

The dough rises on steam alone: it is loaded with water, and in the oven's heat that water flashes into steam and blows the soft dough up like a balloon, hollowing out the middle. It is also the dough you cook twice, for butter and water are boiled, flour is beaten in, and the mixture is cooked into a smooth paste in a saucepan on the hob before it is ever piped and baked.

That stovetop cooking has a purpose, because heating the paste swells and bursts the flour's starch granules, so the dough can absorb far more egg and water than raw flour ever could, and that extra water is the fuel that turns to steam in the oven. Choux can be savoury too: in Burgundy, cooks beat grated Gruyère cheese into the dough to make gougères, cheese puffs served cold with wine in the cellars.

chowder-and-the-tomato-feud.context_blurb:
Clam chowder is New England's great seafood soup, and few dishes start louder arguments. The Boston kind is thick and creamy, the Manhattan kind is red with tomato, and Rhode Island goes its own way. Behind the feud lies a soup older than any of its modern ingredients.

The word comes from chaudière, the big iron cauldron French and Breton fishermen boiled their catch in, so a chowder is named for its pot, not for anything in the bowl.

The first chowders, eaten by colonial New England sailors, had no clams, milk or potatoes, and they were thickened with crumbled ship's biscuit, the rock-hard hardtack sailors carried. A New England clam chowder still begins with salt pork, as the cook renders the diced pork and cooks onions slowly in the drippings before the potatoes and milk go in.

The Boston writer Eleanor Early loathed New York's red, tomato chowder, calling it a terrible pink mixture, and wrote that tomatoes and clams went together no better than ice cream and horseradish. Rhode Island's 'South County' chowder skips both cream and tomato, leaving a clear broth almost as light as stock, made with clams, potatoes, onion and salt pork. The oldest printed chowder recipe, a rhyming poem in a Boston newspaper of 1751, layered fish, pork, onions and hardtack with spices, and poured in red wine. A modern bowl usually comes with oyster crackers on the side.

In 1939 the feud reached Maine's statehouse, where the lawmaker Cleveland Sleeper proposed a bill to outlaw tomatoes in chowder, with a gloriously petty sentence for offenders: they would have to dig a whole barrel of clams when the tide was in, an impossible task since the clam flats are underwater then. The bill never passed, and the quarrel was settled instead by a public cook-off, which the creamy white New England chowder won, with Maine's governor among the judges.

cilantro-tastes-like-soap.context_blurb:
Cilantro, the fresh green leaf of the coriander plant, is loved in salsas, curries and noodle soups around the world. Yet about one person in eight takes a bite and tastes dish soap. Those people are not just being picky. Scientists have traced the reaction partly to their genes, and partly to something else.

The soapy reaction traces to genes for smell, not taste, specifically smell-receptor genes on chromosome 11, so what such people react to is really the herb's aroma rather than anything on the taste buds.

The herb's other name, coriander, comes from the ancient Greek koris, meaning bedbug, because the Greeks thought it smelled like one, and modern chemistry backs them up: the same aldehydes that give cilantro its scent are alarm chemicals that stink bugs spray.

Even the 'cilantro gene', a version of the smell receptor OR6A2, accounts for barely half of one percent of the differences between people, and how much cilantro you ate growing up matters far more, which is why people raised on cilantro-rich cooking rarely taste soap at all.

cinnamon-the-bark-from-ceylon-and-the-bi.context_blurb:
True cinnamon comes from Sri Lanka, the island once called Ceylon. For centuries the merchants who sold it kept its source a secret, spreading wild stories about where it came from, while emperors burned it and trading companies fought over it. The spice was worth fortunes, and almost everything in its history is a story of keeping it rare.

A cinnamon stick is a piece of bark, the dried inner bark of a cinnamon tree, peeled from young branches, and as the thin strip dries it curls into the familiar quill. The true cinnamon tree's native home is Sri Lanka, called Ceylon until 1972, which still grows most of the world's supply.

Most cheap supermarket 'cinnamon' is not that true Ceylon spice but cassia, the darker, thicker, stronger bark of a cousin tree grown mainly in China and Vietnam. Long before Europeans knew where cinnamon grew, Arab middlemen spread the tale of giant cinnamon birds that built nests of it on unclimbable cliffs, a story told to hide the real source and keep its price soaring. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder scoffed that such tales were invented to raise the price.

In ancient Rome a pound of cinnamon could cost a labourer years of wages, and at the funeral of his wife Poppaea in AD 65, the emperor Nero reportedly burned a year's worth of the city's cinnamon, to show off his grief and his wealth. Ceylon's cinnamon forests were so fragrant that, a Dutch captain boasted, sailors downwind of the island could smell the spice on the breeze eight leagues out to sea, about 24 miles.

By 1658 the Dutch East India Company controlled the cinnamon harvest, and to stop the market from ever being flooded it capped how much bark could be peeled and even had surplus cinnamon trees destroyed.

cinnamon-the-bark-that-curls.context_blurb:
A cinnamon stick is a tight brown tube about the size of a finger, and its shape is a clue to everything about it: which part of the tree it is, how it is harvested, and whether it is the true spice or a cheaper cousin. Its history is full of tall tales, told on purpose.

A cinnamon stick is a strip of the tree's inner bark, peeled off and rolled into a tube called a quill. Workers cut a branch, scrape off the rough outer bark, and peel the thin inner layer away in a strip about half a millimetre thick. Laid flat and wet in the sun, the strip curls up on its own into a tight roll within a few hours, with no mould or machine needed. The most prized kind, Cinnamomum verum or 'true cinnamon', takes its old name from Ceylon, as Sri Lanka was once called, the island that still grows most of it.

The jar labelled 'cinnamon' in most kitchens usually holds cassia, a cheaper, bolder relative from China, Indonesia and Vietnam. You can tell them apart by eye: cassia is a thick, hard, dark reddish-brown scroll, like a rolled newspaper, while a true Ceylon stick is pale and thin, built from many soft, papery layers packed together like a cigar, and it crumbles in your hand.

Cassia carries far more coumarin than true cinnamon, about 1 percent against a trace, and coumarin can be hard on the liver in large daily doses; an occasional sprinkle is fine, but Ceylon is the safer choice for someone who eats a lot.

The Greek historian Herodotus told how giant birds built nests of cinnamon on cliffs no one could climb, so the traders left heavy chunks of meat below; the birds carried the meat up, the extra weight broke the nests loose, and the traders gathered the cinnamon that fell. Pliny the Elder, writing in Rome, saw through it, saying traders invented such monsters to raise their prices and hide the real source, which was plain: it came by sea, on merchant ships from the East.

clean-vs-sanitize-two-different-jobs.context_blurb:
In a kitchen, cleaning and sanitising sound like the same job, but they are two different jobs, and neither can stand in for the other. One deals with what you can see; the other deals with life too small to see. Food-safety professionals insist on both, done in a fixed order.

Cleaning removes the crumbs, grease and smears you can see, but a counter that looks spotless can still carry germs too small to see, which survive wiping, and sanitising is the job that cuts those germs down to a safe level. Cleaning must come first, because leftover grease and food scraps form a shield the germs hide under, so a sanitiser sprayed onto a dirty surface cannot reach them, and some sanitisers are even weakened by food residue.

A chemical sanitiser also has to stay wet on the surface for its full contact time, about 10 seconds for bleach and about 30 for iodine, so wiping it dry too soon means it never had time to work. The last step is to let the surface dry in the air, never with a towel, because a towel that has already been used carries its own germs and wipes them straight back onto the clean counter.

cloves-and-the-five-volcanic-spice-islan.context_blurb:
Cloves are the dried buds of a tree that, for most of history, grew in only one place on Earth: a handful of tiny volcanic islands in what is now Indonesia, the Moluccas or Maluku, Europe's fabled Spice Islands. Whoever controlled those islands controlled the world's cloves, and for that prize traders lied, empires fought and whole groves burned.

A whole clove is an unopened flower bud, picked and dried before it could bloom, with four little sepals around a ball of folded petals. Until the 1500s every clove on Earth came from five tiny volcanic islands in the Maluku, Ternate, Tidore, Moti, Makian and Bacan, and nowhere else, which made the spice worth its weight in gold. That scarcity pulled traders from China, Arabia and at last Europe halfway around the world.

The English name comes from the Latin clavus, a nail, because a dried clove looks just like a tiny dark nail, and Chinese cooks saw the same thing, naming it 'nail-shaped fragrance'. Courtiers of China's Han emperors, more than twenty centuries ago, had to hold a clove in the mouth before speaking to the emperor, to sweeten the breath. On the islands themselves, a family planted a clove tree when a child was born and treated it as the child's own, believing the tree's health mirrored the child's fate.

Arab and Asian traders guarded the islands' location so fiercely that Europe filled the gap with legend, including the tale that only genies, working by magic, could grow and pick cloves. The Dutch East India Company, master of the islands from the mid-1600s, wanted cloves scarce, so from 1652 its soldiers cut down and burned every clove tree outside the company's own plantations, many of them the islanders' birth trees. To the islanders it felt like an attack on their own children, and they fought fiercely to save the trees. Around 1770 a Frenchman smuggled clove and nutmeg seedlings past the Dutch and broke the monopoly for good, and his name, fittingly, was Pierre Poivre, French for pepper. The smuggled trees thrived across the Indian Ocean on Zanzibar, off East Africa, which became the world's clove capital in the 1800s.

Dentists dab clove oil on a sore tooth for good reason: the oil's main compound, eugenol, blocks the tiny channels a nerve uses to fire its pain signal, the same channels that local anaesthetics target, so the message never reaches the brain. Dentists still mix eugenol with zinc oxide to make a soothing temporary filling.

cloves-the-unopened-flower-bud.context_blurb:
Each clove in the jar is a little dark spike with a ball on its head. It is one of the strongest spices in the kitchen, used whole to stud a Christmas ham or perfume a stock, and its power comes from catching the plant at exactly the right moment. A picker who is late ruins it.

That ball is a flower bud, picked while still closed, just before it would have opened, and its head is four unopened petals balled up; the buds are dried in the sun from bright red to dark brown. Garlic cloves are no relation, for the spice's name comes from the Latin clavus and the Old French clou, both meaning a nail, because a dried clove is shaped like a tiny brown nail with a round head.

For hundreds of years every clove came from a few tiny volcanic islands, the northern Maluku, Europe's Spice Islands, which today belong to Indonesia. A bitten clove leaves the gum tingly and then numb, and that power comes from the fragrant oil packed inside it, mostly a compound called eugenol, which old-time dentists dabbed on aching teeth.

One clove packs such a punch that cooks use them whole and take them out again: a ham studded with cloves, or an onion spiked with a couple of them to season a stock and then thrown away, flavours the dish without making it bitter or medicinal.

cochinita-pibil-and-the-underground-oven.context_blurb:
Cochinita pibil comes from the Yucatán, the Maya heartland of south-eastern Mexico, and it is pork roasted slowly for hours. The meat is marinated in a bright orange paste, wrapped in leaves and cooked for hours, traditionally in a pit in the ground, until it falls apart at a touch. Its ingredients and even its name tell the story of Maya cooking meeting Spanish farm animals.

'Cochinita' means a little or baby pig, from the Spanish cochino, and the most traditional version roasts a whole young suckling pig. The meat is wrapped in banana leaves, which trap the steam and perfume the pork as it cooks.

Its sunset-orange colour comes from achiote paste, ground from the seed also called annatto, which is rubbed onto the raw meat; it tastes mild, sweet and a little peppery, and it is neither chilli nor tomato.

The marinade is thinned with the juice of the Seville orange, the sour or bitter orange valued in the Yucatán for its sharp bite rather than its sweetness. The truly traditional cooking happens in a piib, the Maya earth oven: a pit lined with hardwood and stones and fired until the stones glow, then loaded with the leaf-wrapped bundle and buried under earth to roast low and slow. Piib means 'buried', and it gives the dish the second half of its name.

The English word barbecue comes from barbacoa, a Taíno word first printed in Spanish in 1526, which originally meant a framework of green sticks raised over a fire to cook or cure meat; in Mexico the Spanish later used it for pit cooking. Pork itself is a newcomer, since pigs reached the Yucatán only on Spanish ships in the 1500s; earlier Maya cooks made the same buried-pit dish with wild turkey, or with deer.

Achiote travels the world under the name annatto, and the very seed that turns the pork orange also colours orange Cheddar, Red Leicester and other cheeses, and even some butter.

coffee-crosses-to-the-new-world.context_blurb:
Coffee is one of the few great crops that crossed the Atlantic the 'wrong' way. Potatoes, tomatoes and cacao sailed out of the Americas to feed the world, but coffee sailed in. Today the Americas grow a huge share of the world's coffee, from a plant that never grew wild there.

The wild coffee shrub grows in the highlands of Ethiopia, and the drink was first brewed across the Red Sea in Yemen, so coffee was an Old World plant from the start.

In 1720 the French naval officer Gabriel de Clieu brought one coffee plant across the Atlantic to Martinique, in the Caribbean, and he is remembered for sharing his own ration of drinking water with it to keep it alive on the long voyage. The plant thrived and helped stock the Caribbean's coffee estates.

Brazil now grows about a third of all the world's coffee, far more than any other country, though the plant is not native there; a Portuguese officer, Francisco de Melo Palheta, planted Brazil's first coffee bush in 1727.

coffees-hidden-ferment-your-morning-bean.context_blurb:
Most people picture coffee as dry brown beans, roasted and ground. Few coffee drinkers know that the bean is really a seed taken from a juicy fruit, and that on many farms it spends a day or two being fermented, a little like grapes for wine, before it is ever dried and roasted.

The coffee bush bears no beans: it bears little shiny fruits, green at first and red when ripe, that growers call coffee cherries, and the 'bean' is the seed inside.

In washed coffee, growers press off the red skin, but each seed still wears a sticky, sugary coat called mucilage. So they soak the seeds in tanks of water for a day or two while wild microbes feast on that sugar and ferment the coat away, until the seeds feel rough and pebbly instead of slimy.

Most cherries hold two seeds pressed flat against each other, which is why a coffee bean has one flat side, but now and then only one seed grows, and with no twin to flatten it, it becomes a small, round bean called a peaberry. Roasters often sort peaberries out and sell them on their own.

cold-is-a-brake-not-a-kill-fridge-and-fr.context_blurb:
A fridge and a freezer both make food last longer, but neither one kills the germs that spoil food or make people sick. Cold works as a brake, not an off switch. The moment food warms up again, the germs pick up where they left off, and that one idea explains most of the rules of safe cold storage.

At 40°F or below, a fridge only slows bacteria down, so they grow very slowly or not at all, but they stay alive and at work, which is why even cold leftovers spoil in the end. Freezing to 0°F stops their growth completely, yet it does not kill them either, because the germs fall into a dormant state and wake up again when the food thaws, so thawed food is only as safe as it was when it went in.

Freezer burn, the dry, leathery, greyish-brown patches on a forgotten steak, happens when air reaches the surface and pulls out moisture; the food is still safe to eat, only dry in those spots, so you can simply cut them away.

The fridge door is the warmest, most changeable spot, because it swings open more than anywhere else, so milk and eggs belong on a cold inside shelf, while sturdy ketchup, pickles and jam cope with the door just fine. Never thaw a frozen turkey on the counter, because while its middle is still frozen, its surface warms above 40°F into the danger zone of 40 to 140°F, where bacteria multiply fastest, doubling in as little as 20 minutes. Thaw it slowly in the fridge instead.

collagen-and-gelatin-the-protein-in-bone.context_blurb:
Collagen is the body's most plentiful protein, and the animals we eat are built from it too. It is the tough scaffolding of skin, tendons and bones. Long, gentle heat turns it into something soft and wobbly, and that change gives bone broth its body, gummy bears their chew and a panna cotta the strength to stand up.

In a steak, the collagen is the chewy gristle that runs through the meat, part of the stringy glue that binds skin, tendons, bones and cartilage together.

Simmer bones and knuckles slowly for hours and the heat unravels their collagen and dissolves it into gelatin, which is why the strained broth sets overnight into trembling jelly; the change starts around 160°F, so braising liquid is kept at a gentle simmer.

Gelatin is simply collagen that heat has unravelled, drawn from the skin, bones and connective tissue of animals such as pigs, cattle and fish, so the chew of a Haribo gummy bear, first sold by Hans Riegel in Bonn in 1922, comes from animal collagen. A spoonful of gelatin can set a bowl of cream into panna cotta because it traps five to ten times its own weight in water, weaving the water into a wobbling web called a hydrogel.

columbus-sailed-for-spices-and-hit-a-hem.context_blurb:
When Christopher Columbus left Spain with three small ships in August 1492, he was not out to prove that the Earth was round. He was looking for a sea route to the spice markets of Asia. Instead he reached a whole hemisphere that Europeans did not know existed, and started the greatest food swap in history.

What Columbus wanted most was spice, black pepper, cinnamon and cloves, the luxuries of Asia's markets, and he gambled that sailing west would be a shortcut to the 'Indies'; on 12 October he landed not in Asia but on an island in the Bahamas. In the Caribbean his men met allspice, which is not a mixture at all but a single dried berry that tastes of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once.

Columbus never found the black pepper he was hunting, but when he tasted the Caribbean's fiery red pods, the only thing he knew that burned like them was the peppercorn, so he called them pepper too. That is why English still says 'chilli pepper', and German 'Pfeffer', for a plant unrelated to the pepper vine. His voyage launched the Columbian Exchange, the two-way swap of foods between the hemispheres: chocolate, chilli, tomatoes and potatoes sailed east to the Old World, while wheat, sugar, citrus and coffee came west into American kitchens.

Long before anyone called them peppers, the Taíno islanders called the chilli aji, and Diego Álvarez Chanca, the doctor on Columbus's second voyage, wrote home that they seasoned their bread and fish with it, the earliest eyewitness account of anyone cooking with chilli.

confit-and-cassoulet.context_blurb:
Confit is the great preserving trick of southwestern France. Before refrigerators, farm cooks in Gascony and the Languedoc kept duck and goose through the winter by cooking the meat gently in its own fat and storing it there. The word comes from the French confire, "to preserve", and the meat ends up in one of France's most famous country dishes, cassoulet.

To make confit, the cook lays salted duck legs in a pot and pours melted fat over them until they are completely covered. The fat is kept gentle, around 85°C, far below the heat of a deep-fryer, so the meat poaches quietly for hours and never crisps or turns brown. Gascon cooks are strict about one thing: true confit is made only from the legs of the duck or goose. Give any other cut, or a different bird, the same slow bath and the result is merely "en confit", a copy rather than the real dish.

Confit was invented to keep meat, not just to flavour it. Once cooked, the legs were packed into a crock and covered with more fat, which set into a hard, thick cap. That cap shuts the meat away from the air completely, and with no oxygen able to reach it, the meat cannot spoil. Kept cool and dark in a cellar, a crock of confit could last about three months.

The fat cap is only half the secret. A full day before the legs meet any fat, the cook packs them in salt and herbs, and the salt draws water out of the meat, starting a cure that holds back bacteria. Together, salt and fat let a duck survive a winter with no fridge.

In the Languedoc, confit goes into cassoulet, a slow-baked feast built around white beans, the humble haricot, layered with duck or goose confit, sausage and pork. The beans cost far less than the meat, but they are the heart of the dish: they drink up the rich fat over hours in the oven and give the cassoulet its body.

Even the dish's name comes from the kitchen, because cassoulet is named for the cassole, the pot of red clay that it is baked in. The cassole is shaped like a cone, wide at the mouth and narrow at the base, and was first made in the village of Issel, near Castelnaudary, where potters still shape it by hand. Its wide mouth gives the beans the biggest surface for a prized golden crust.

cooking-changes-nutrition-both-direction.context_blurb:
Is raw food healthier than cooked food? Folk wisdom often says yes, and folk wisdom is only half right. Heat in a kitchen works in both directions: it destroys some nutrients, washes others away, and frees many that raw food keeps locked up. It even disarms some natural poisons.

Start with the tomato, whose red colour comes from lycopene, an antioxidant that helps the body fight disease. In 2002 the Cornell food scientist Rui Hai Liu heated tomatoes to about 88°C, and after thirty minutes the usable lycopene had soared by 164 percent, because heat breaks down the tough cell walls that hold the pigment in. That is why a cooked sauce or canned tomatoes can beat a raw slice. Broccoli goes the other way. Vitamin C and the B vitamins dissolve in water, so when broccoli tumbles at a hard boil in a big pot, those vitamins leak out into the water and go down the drain when the cook empties it. A hard boil can wash out nearly all of the vitamin C, while steaming, which keeps the florets out of the water, saves roughly four-fifths. Steam it, don't drown it.

The Cornell tomatoes paid a price as well. The same heating that raised their lycopene cut their vitamin C by 29 percent, close to a third, because vitamin C is fragile in heat as well as soluble in water, so it is the first nutrient to go when produce is cooked. Carrots show how cooking can free a nutrient instead. Their orange pigment, beta-carotene, is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin A, but a raw carrot gives up only about 11 percent of it. Heat ruptures the stiff walls of the plant cells where the pigment is locked away, so a stir-fried carrot gives up about 75 percent, and a little oil at the same meal helps even more.

Protein follows the same rule. A cooked egg's protein is more than 90 percent digestible, a raw egg's only 50 to 60 percent, so the film boxer Rocky Balboa, gulping raw eggs, wasted much of what he swallowed. Heat unfolds the tangled protein molecules so that the digestive enzymes in your gut can reach them and cut them apart. Starch is locked up even tighter, since the gut can draw only about half the energy out of raw potato starch. Cooking makes the tiny starch granules in each potato cell soak up water, swell and burst open, a change called gelatinization, and the burst starch lies open to the digestive enzymes. In 2011 Rachel Carmody and Richard Wrangham at Harvard showed the result in mice: mice fed raw sweet potato actually lost weight, while mice fed the identical food cooked gained, because the heat itself had unlocked usable calories that the raw food kept to itself.

People often say that cooking spinach unlocks its iron, but that iron is the plant kind, non-heme iron, which the body absorbs poorly however the spinach is cooked. Spinach's oxalic acid, long blamed for blocking iron, actually grips calcium far harder, which is why spinach makes a poor calcium source despite its healthy green look. The real trick for spinach's iron is vitamin C at the same meal: a good squeeze of lemon on the plate helps the body take in two or three times as much iron.

Some foods are dangerous raw for reasons that have nothing to do with germs. Raw red kidney beans carry phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin that the bean plant makes itself as a natural defense, and a mere handful of raw beans can set off violent vomiting within hours. The safe way is to soak dried kidney beans, then bring them to a full, rolling boil in a fresh pot of water at 100°C and keep them there for at least thirty minutes. Only that fierce, wet heat breaks the toxin down, and a slow cooker on a low setting, at around 80°C, can leave the beans several times more toxic than raw ones. Raw egg white has a trap of its own. Its protein avidin clamps onto biotin, one of the B vitamins, with a grip tighter than any other bond of its type in nature, so the vitamin passes through the body unused. Cooking the egg until the white sets breaks the trap: above about 70°C the avidin unfolds, and by about 85°C it lets the vitamin go.
